text_summary.body: Josiah gathered the elders, read the book of the covenant in the Temple and made a covenant by the pillar. He had the vessels made for Baal, Asherah and the host of heaven burned in the Kidron fields; removed the idolatrous priests; burned the Asherah; broke down the shrine-prostitutes' houses; defiled the high places from Geba to Beersheba and Topheth in the valley of Hinnom; removed the horses and chariots of the sun; broke the roof altars of Ahaz and Manasseh's altars; and defiled Solomon's high places for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom.

setting.period: c. 628–621 BC (Chronicles' 12th year to Kings' 18th year)
setting.body: Keil argues that the purge began before the book was found (2 Chr 34:3, the twelfth year) and was completed afterwards, the narrative grouping everything under the eighteenth year. Guzik quotes Patterson and Austel that horses in sun-worship are attested in Assyrian and Aramean sources (not checked here).

assumptions: Applies to the covenant ceremony; Keil and 2 Chr 34:3 place the beginning of the purge earlier.

locations.role: Temple, Kidron, Topheth, the Mount of Corruption

terminology.gloss: A term for non-Yahwistic priests (23:5; Zeph 1:4; Hos 10:5); Clarke's etymology (via Guzik) is not adopted.
Cult place in the valley of Hinnom associated with child sacrifice to Molech (23:10; Jer 7:31).

competing_reconstructions.label: Reform spread over several years and grouped under the 18th year by subject
competing_reconstructions.summary: The covenant could not have been made with idolatrous altars still standing in the Temple; the purge began earlier and was completed after the discovery.

competing_reconstructions.label: All of 2 Kgs 22:3–23:23 within the 18th year
proponents: J. Ussher (as reported by Keil), placing the Passover at the close of the 18th year
competing_reconstructions.summary: Takes the two "eighteenth year" statements (22:3; 23:23) as bracketing a single year.

commentary.paraphrase: Guzik compares the covenant with Mizpah and Shechem (after Wiseman) and reads the reform as moving from the Temple outward; he notes that the people's turning was outward conformity (Jer 3:10).
